the visual system is biased toward attending to objects that are relevant to the observer’s task.
the spatial scale of attention is controlled by task demands, and the degree of task engagement controls the degree of exogenous influence.

understanding the role of attention in visual perception and cognition.

the theory provides a new framework for thinking about attention, and that it is supported by a large and growing body of empirical data.
the theory offers a novel perspective on visual attention that emphasizes the importance of experience and task knowledge in the control of attention.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have proposed a unified theory of attention, which can be used to explain the diverse range of phenomena in the literature.
the human visual system is not a passive sensor but an active, goal-directed system, and the attentional system is a critical component of that goal-directed system.
attention is not a fixed, pre-wired mechanism, but a dynamic, experience-dependent process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanisms of attention are not fixed, but rather are flexible and can adapt to the demands of the current task.
attention is not a fixed mechanism, but rather a dynamic system that is constantly changing in response to the demands of the task at hand.
attention is fundamentally a process of knowledge-based selection, rather than feature-based competition.
